Shared-pool resampling preserves uniform marginals, but changes the joint distribution. Let N be the eligible catalog size: draw M IID uniform pool items, then K pool indices with replacement. Conditional on the pool, negatives are IID from its empirical distribution; unconditionally, they are dependent, as in [bootstrap resampling](https://www.stat.purdue.edu/~dasgupta/bootstrap.pdf). For two negatives, P(equal)=1/M+(1−1/M)/N, versus 1/N for direct IID draws. For any fixed item-score function f, their covariance is Var[f(U)]/M. Sharing the pool across examples also correlates their sampling noise.

For K=16, M=64, the expected number of distinct selected pool slots is 64[1−(63/64)^16]=14.255; probability of repeating a slot is 87.10%; expected matching-slot pairs is 120/64=1.875. Distinct item counts can be lower because the pool itself permits duplicates. Direct IID sampling has expected distinct count N[1−(1−1/N)^16]. Repeated negatives retain multiplicity: m copies contribute m·exp(s), equivalent to one denominator term with logit s+log(m). [Sampled-softmax formulations explicitly retain repeated classes](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/blanc18a/blanc18a.pdf).

Analytically, for fixed scores, let Z=exp(s(U)−s_positive), with loss L=log(1+ΣZ). Both schemes have the same expected denominator, but shared-pool sampling increases sum variance by 1+(K−1)/M=1.234375. More strongly, conditioning on repeated-slot groups shows a mean-preserving spread relative to IID; concavity therefore gives E[L_pool]≤E[L_IID], generally strictly for nonconstant scores. Thus it changes the expected objective, not merely gradient noise. To match an IID control, draw directly, or select K distinct slots from the IID pool; the latter also yields IID catalog items. Hold eligibility filtering and loss corrections fixed.
